source.evidence_summary: A filter scores subsets independently of the final learner before training; a wrapper evaluates subsets using the learner's predictive performance, making it more model-specific and computationally expensive.

reference_answer: An excellent answer should establish: filter uses learner-independent criterion; wrapper evaluates with learner; wrapper is model-specific and costlier.

conversation_history.content: Filter versus wrapper—what changes in the actual workflow?

A filter selects features before model training using a separate criterion such as correlation or information. A wrapper repeatedly trains and evaluates the intended learner on candidate subsets, so it can capture model-specific effects but costs much more.

reference_answer: An excellent answer should establish: Spearman uses ranks; appropriate for ordinal/monotonic association; Pearson measures linear numeric association.

conversation_history.content: Filter versus wrapper—what changes in the actual workflow?

A filter selects features before model training using a separate criterion such as correlation or information. A wrapper repeatedly trains and evaluates the intended learner on candidate subsets, so it can capture model-specific effects but costs much more.
When would I use Spearman instead of Pearson here?

Use Spearman when the variables are ordinal or their relationship is monotonic but not necessarily linear, since it correlates ranks. Pearson is appropriate when a linear relationship between numerical values is the quantity of interest.

Let 'positive' mean the patient truly has the disease. A true positive is sick and predicted sick; a false positive is healthy but predicted sick; a false negative is sick but predicted healthy; and a true negative is healthy and predicted healthy.

conversation_history.content: Can you map TP, FP, FN, and TN to a medical test example?

Let 'positive' mean the patient truly has the disease. A true positive is sick and predicted sick; a false positive is healthy but predicted sick; a false negative is sick but predicted healthy; and a true negative is healthy and predicted healthy.
I keep swapping precision and recall. What's the cleanest way to remember them?

Precision asks, 'Of everything I called positive, how much was truly positive?' Recall asks, 'Of everything truly positive, how much did I find?' Their denominators are predicted positives and actual positives, respectively.

conversation_history.content: Holdout and cross-validation—when is the second worth the extra work?

Holdout trains and tests once, so it is cheap but its estimate can depend heavily on that split. Cross-validation rotates the test fold across several runs, usually giving a more stable use of limited data at the cost of repeated training.

user_utterance: Why can 99% accuracy still be useless?
canonical_question: Explain why accuracy can be misleading under severe class imbalance.

retrieval.context: Course evidence (Evaluation_Unit_1_Basics(3).pdf, physical PDF page(s) 34, 35, 36, 37, 38, 39, 40, 41): A classifier can achieve 99% accuracy by always predicting a 99% majority class while detecting none of the rare class; class-specific metrics and costs are needed.

source.evidence_summary: A classifier can achieve 99% accuracy by always predicting a 99% majority class while detecting none of the rare class; class-specific metrics and costs are needed.

reference_answer: An excellent answer should establish: majority-only classifier example; rare-class failures hidden by accuracy; use precision/recall/F-measure or costs.

conversation_history.content: Holdout and cross-validation—when is the second worth the extra work?

Holdout trains and tests once, so it is cheap but its estimate can depend heavily on that split. Cross-validation rotates the test fold across several runs, usually giving a more stable use of limited data at the cost of repeated training.
Why can 99% accuracy still be useless?

If 99% of records are negative, predicting 'negative' every time already gives 99% accuracy while recall for the rare positive class is zero. You therefore inspect precision, recall, F-measure, and possibly misclassification costs.

conversation_history.content: What is the difference between a good model and the best model?

A model is 'good' if its performance is meaningfully better than a baseline or meets the task requirement. Calling one 'best' requires a fair comparison against alternatives using the same data, metric, and uncertainty analysis.

conversation_history.content: What is the difference between a good model and the best model?

A model is 'good' if its performance is meaningfully better than a baseline or meets the task requirement. Calling one 'best' requires a fair comparison against alternatives using the same data, metric, and uncertainty analysis.
Why isn't the larger observed score enough to pick it?

Because each score is an estimate from a finite test sample. A small observed gap may be sampling noise, so you examine confidence intervals or an appropriate significance test before claiming a real performance difference.

conversation_history.content: Model A got 85% on 30 cases, and B got 75% on 5,000. Is A really better?

A has the larger point estimate, but 30 cases produce a wide uncertainty interval compared with 5,000. You cannot responsibly call A better from those percentages alone; calculate the confidence interval for the difference using the actual counts and test design.

conversation_history.content: Model A got 85% on 30 cases, and B got 75% on 5,000. Is A really better?

A has the larger point estimate, but 30 cases produce a wide uncertainty interval compared with 5,000. You cannot responsibly call A better from those percentages alone; calculate the confidence interval for the difference using the actual counts and test design.
And if I'm comparing six algorithms across several datasets, can I just run every pairwise test?

Not without correcting for multiple comparisons. The course workflow first applies a Friedman test to the algorithms' ranks across datasets; if that rejects equal performance, a post-hoc procedure such as Nemenyi identifies which pairs differ.
